analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from adding new regulatory burdens unless they first repeal two existing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill had one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in March 2023, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The RED Tape Act would have imposed a 'two-for-one' rule on federal agencies: before an agency could issue any new rule that creates a financial or administrative burden on businesses or the public, it would have to repeal or amend two or more existing burden-creating rules, and the new rule's cost could not exceed the cost of the rules repealed. It would also have required agencies to publish their planned rulemakings and costs twice a year and let the agency head certify cost equivalence. The bill was introduced by Sen. Dan Sullivan with one cosponsor, referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that bear the cost of complying with federal regulations, especially industries facing new rules on safety, health, environment, or finances. By capping the total 'burden' agencies can impose, the bill would make it harder to issue any new protective rule, which reduces compliance costs for regulated firms.

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies to repeal or amend two or more existing 'covered rules' before issuing any new rule that imposes a financial or administrative burden on businesses or people, and requires the new rule's cost to be no greater than the cost of the rules repealed [S2][S3].

Defines 'rule' broadly to include rules issued under executive orders, memoranda, guidance documents, bulletins, and even press releases, so the two-for-one requirement would reach informal agency actions that businesses otherwise challenge as backdoor regulation [S3].
Requires agencies to publish semiannual lists of rules they intend to issue or repeal, along with each rule's cost, and bars them from issuing rules until they comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of the public who rely on federal rules for protection — worker safety, food and drug safety, environmental quality, consumer finance — because any new protective rule would require the agency to eliminate two existing rules first, regardless of whether the new rule's benefits exceed its costs. Agency heads themselves certify the cost comparisons, so there is no outside check.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The bill does not weigh benefits against costs when deciding which rules to repeal: the repeal requirement turns on matching costs, and the statute lists benefit considerations only as factors the agency head 'shall consider' in choosing which rules to repeal, not as a veto [S3].

A rigid two-for-one cap means a rule addressing a new hazard could be blocked unless an agency retires two existing rules, slowing or preventing responses to emergent safety, health, or environmental problems [S3].

The agency head itself determines which rules count as burden-creating and certifies that the new rule costs no more than the repealed ones, so the constraint depends entirely on the agency's own accounting [S3].
The bill exempts rules covering the agency's own internal policy or procurement, so agencies' internal burdens are not subject to the cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters would argue the bill forces agencies to think about obsolete or overlapping rules and gives businesses predictable limits on new compliance costs. The honest counterweight: the bill caps regulatory burden by cost alone, without requiring that the rules repealed be less valuable than the new one, so a high-benefit new protection could be traded away for two low-benefit repeals. The certification process is self-administered by each agency head, which makes both the discipline and the risk depend on who holds the pen.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on March 7, 2023, with Sen. Steve Daines as its single cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day; that was the bill's last action [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and neither chamber voted on it before the 118th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, agencies kept their existing authority to issue new rules without a two-for-one repeal requirement, and the public kept the possibility of new protections. Businesses seeking a hard cap on new regulatory burdens are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public kept current rules

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, though the committee simply never acted rather than voting it down.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses broadly (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other firms subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would cap the total new compliance burden agencies can impose, lowering costs for regulated firms. The offset is that new protective rules — on safety, health, environment, or consumer finance — could be issued only by retiring existing ones, so the industry's gain comes at the price of weaker public protections.

Small firms often bear disproportionate per-employee compliance costs, so a burden cap would help them. The same cap could delay rules that protect small firms' workers, products, or access to credit.

Agencies would lose discretion to issue burden-creating rules, including informal guidance, without offsetting repeals, and would face new semiannual public reporting of planned rules and their costs. Supporters view this as accountability; critics view it as a straitjacket on responding to new problems.
